title: Self-Reflection in Relationships
keyIdea: Reflecting on a friendship means looking at your own part, not only at what others do. Look for patterns: things you do again and again, like always choosing the game or staying quiet when you disagree. Most habits help in the right amount and cause problems when there is too much or too little. Name what you do well as well as what to work on. Then turn one pattern into a goal you can check: when, and what you will do.

kid: When a friendship goes wrong, it is easy to look only at the other person. Reflecting means asking: what is my part? Not to blame yourself, but because your part is the bit you can change.

Start with patterns. One time is just a moment. A pattern is something you do again and again. If you picked the game on Monday, Wednesday and Friday, that is a pattern. Thinking back over a week helps you see it.

Most habits are not simply good or bad. Taking the lead gets a group started. Too much, and others stop sharing ideas. Letting small things go keeps the peace. Always staying quiet means friends never know what you want.

Be fair to yourself. Name a strength, like keeping secrets or saying sorry, and one stretch to work on. Then make a goal you can check: At break, I will ask two friends what they want to play before I suggest a game.
adult: This topic is part of self-awareness and relationship skills in the CASEL framework. The PSHE Association programme for Key Stage 2 asks pupils to say what makes a good friendship. It also asks them to think about their own behaviour in it. At 9 to 11, children can start to see their own habits from the outside.

Three ideas carry the topic. A pattern is a habit seen across many moments, so one incident is weak evidence. Most social habits, like leading, going along and talking about yourself, help in the right amount and cause harm at either extreme. A useful goal is specific and easy to check. Researchers call this an implementation intention: when this happens, I will do that.

Common mistakes: treating one incident as a pattern; labelling the whole self (I am bossy) instead of naming an action; listing only faults, which lowers mood but rarely changes much; swinging to the other extreme (never lead again); blaming the other person; and setting vague goals such as be nicer.

In the lab, learners tally six moments from one week until a pattern shows. They slide three habits to find the amount that works for friends. They sort Priya's notes into strengths and stretches, and choose goals they could check tomorrow.

familyTip: At dinner, each person shares one thing they did well with a friend this week and one thing they might do differently. Help your child turn the second one into a when, I will goal, and ask how it went a few days later.

visual.caption: Is each goal one you could check tomorrow, or too vague? Drag each goal to a box, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: At lunch, I will ask one friend how their day was
When I disagree, I will say so once, calmly
In group work, I will let two people speak before me

lab.caption: Flagship lab: tally your moments to find a pattern, slide habits to the right amount, sort strengths and stretches, and choose a goal you can check.

practice.prompt: Which of these is a pattern?
choices: Ella forgets her friend's turn in most games
Ella forgot her friend's turn once
Ella is a bad friend
practice.hint: A pattern happens again and again. Does it name an action?
practice.explain: Most games means again and again, and it names an action Ella can change. Once is a moment, and a bad friend is a label.

practice.prompt: Over a week, Kai decided for the group {a} times and asked others {b} times. How many moments did he look back on?
practice.hint: Add the two kinds of moment together.
practice.explain: {a} times deciding plus {b} times asking makes {=a+b} moments to look back on.

practice.prompt: Ava always stays quiet when she disagrees with friends. What is the best goal?
choices: When I disagree with a plan, I will say once, kindly, what I would like
Always argue back
Be braver
practice.hint: Pick a goal that says when and what, and does not swing too far.
practice.explain: It says when (I disagree with a plan) and what (say it once, kindly). Always argue back goes too far, and be braver is too vague to check.

practice.prompt: Priya writes {a} notes about herself. {b} are strengths. How many are stretches?
practice.hint: Take the strengths away from all the notes.
practice.explain: {a} notes take away {b} strengths leaves {=a-b} stretches to work on.

pool.prompt: What does reflecting on a friendship mean?
choices: Looking at your own part in it, and what you could change
Working out who is to blame
Deciding you are a bad friend
pool.hint: Which part of a friendship can you change?
pool.explain: Reflecting looks at your own part, because that is the part you can change. It is not about blame.

pool.prompt: Leo talks about himself a lot. Which is the right amount of sharing?
choices: Sharing his news and asking about theirs
Never sharing anything
Only talking about himself
pool.hint: Too little and too much both cause problems.
pool.explain: Sharing and asking back is the middle. Never sharing makes him hard to know, and only talking about himself pushes friends away.

pool.prompt: Which is a fair strength to name?
choices: I say sorry when I get it wrong
I am the best friend ever
I am never good at anything
pool.hint: A strength is something real you do.
pool.explain: Saying sorry is a real action you can keep doing. A boast or a put-down is not honest reflection.

pool.prompt: Sam notices he takes over in group work. What is a goal that keeps his strength?
choices: In group work, I will ask for two ideas before I share mine
Never give ideas again
Be less bossy
pool.hint: Keep the strength and change the amount.
pool.explain: Asking first still lets Sam lead. Never giving ideas throws a strength away, and be less bossy is too vague.

pool.prompt: A friend says you never listen. What is a good first step?
choices: Ask for an example and think if it is a pattern
Say she is wrong
Stop being her friend
pool.hint: Check what you do before you decide.
pool.explain: An example helps you check for a pattern. Arguing or walking away stops you learning about your own part.

pool.prompt: Why is “I am bossy” less useful than “I often choose the game without asking”?
choices: It labels you instead of naming an action you can change
It is too long
It is about games
pool.hint: Which one tells you what to change?
pool.explain: A label sounds fixed. Naming the action shows exactly what to do differently.

pool.prompt: Jo kept her goal on {a} of the 5 school days. On how many days did she miss it?
pool.hint: Take the days she kept it away from 5.
pool.explain: 5 days take away {a} days kept leaves {=5-a} days missed. A checkable goal lets her count this.

pool.prompt: Mia tallied her week. She went along with others {a} times, which was {b} times more than she said what she wanted. How many times did she say what she wanted?
pool.hint: Take the difference away from the bigger number.
pool.explain: {a} take away {b} is {=a-b}, so she said what she wanted {=a-b} times. Going along is her pattern.

pool.prompt: Which goal can you check tomorrow?
choices: At break, I will invite one person who is alone to join
Be nice to everyone
Try harder with friends
pool.hint: Does it say when, and what you will do?
pool.explain: It says when (at break) and what (invite one person), so you can tell if you did it.
